::: {.lead}
Today you build a monthly budget in Excel, like in a lab. Each experiment
has two parts. **Part A** is in Excel on the lab computer. **Part B** is on
a simulator of the interactive lesson: on paper, scan its QR code; on the
screen, click its link. After each step, write your result in its box. At
the end, copy your key results into the table.
:::

## Before you start

- **You need:** a computer with Excel (the desktop app, or Excel on the web
  at `office.com`).
- **No lab computer today?** Do Part B of each experiment on your phone. Do
  Part A later on any computer with Excel.
- **Made-up numbers only:** this is the budget of Lina, a made-up student.
  Your real money is private.
- **Check:** the results are at the end of this worksheet. Look only after
  you try. On the interactive lesson, every step has a check that answers
  at once.

## Experiment 1 · The layout and the totals

**The idea:** a **budget** plans the money of one month: what comes in
(**income**) and what goes out (**expenses**). Make two blocks on one
sheet, Income at the top and Expenses below, each with a **Total** line,
and one empty row between them. Column A has the names, column B the
amounts. "JD" goes in the heading, not in the cells. **=SUM** adds each
block, and *Left* is the total income minus the total expenses.

**Aim:** lay out a budget in two blocks, and let Excel add it up.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (Excel)**
:::

1. Open a **Blank workbook**. Type Lina's month: in A1 **Income** and in B1
   **Amount (JD)**; A2 **Allowance**, B2 **120**; A3 **Tutoring**, B3
   **80**; A4 **Total income**. Leave row 5 empty. A6 **Expenses**; A7 to
   A11: **Transport 30**, **Phone 10**, **Food 70**, **Books 20**, **Fun
   20** (the amounts in B7 to B11); A12 **Total expenses**. A14 **Left**.

   {{< record "The rows of the two blocks: income … to … ; expenses … to …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Income** in rows 2–3 with its total in row 4; **expenses** in rows
   7–11 with their total in row 12; **Left** in row 14. The cells of
   column B hold only numbers.
   :::

   ::: {.order}
   Put the rows of a budget in order, from the top of the sheet.

   1. the heading Income
   2. the income amounts
   3. Total income
   4. an empty row
   5. the expenses
   6. Total expenses
   7. Left

   Why: Two blocks, each with its Total line, then what is left.
   :::

2. In B4 type **=SUM(B2:B3)**, in B12 **=SUM(B7:B11)** and in B14
   **=B4-B12**.

   {{< record "Total income … ; total expenses … ; left …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   Total income **200** (120 + 80), total expenses **150** (30 + 10 + 70 +
   20 + 20), left **50** (200 − 150).
   :::

   ::: {.fill answer="50" unit="JD" hint="Total income minus total expenses."}
   Lina's total income is 200 JD and her total expenses are 150 JD. What
   does B14 show with `=B4-B12`?

   Why: 200 − 150 = 50 JD left to save.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="../../week-06/sims/budget-builder.html" poster="../../week-06/sims/budget-builder.png" title="Budget Builder: Sami's month" >}}

3. In **Budget Builder**, build Sami's month: do the first three tasks
   (the total income, the total expenses and what is left).

   {{< record "Sami: income … ; expenses … ; left …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   Total income **250** (=SUM(B2:B3)), total expenses **195**
   (=SUM(B7:B11)), left **55** (=B4-B12).
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Which formula gives what is left in B14?

   - [x] `=B4-B12`

     Why: The total income minus the total expenses.

   - [ ] `=B4+B12`

     Why: Left is what stays after the expenses: subtract them.

   - [ ] `=SUM(B2:B12)`

     Why: That adds the income and the expenses together.
   :::

## Experiment 2 · The part of the income

**The idea:** each expense is a part of the income: divide its amount by
the total income. In C7 write **=B7/\$B\$4** and copy it down with the fill
handle: B7 moves to B8, B9 …; **\$B\$4** (the total income) stays. If one
amount changes, every total and every part changes by itself.

**Aim:** find the part of each expense, and see a budget change by itself.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (Excel)**
:::

1. In C6 type **Part**. In C7 type **=B7/\$B\$4** and copy it down to C11
   with the fill handle. Read C9, the part of food.

   {{< record "C9 shows … ; its formula is …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   C9 shows **0.35** (70 ÷ 200) with **=B9/\$B\$4**: B9 moved with the
   row, and \$B\$4 stayed.
   :::

   ::: {.fill answer="0.35" hint="Food is 70, and the total income is 200."}
   What does C9 show with `=B9/$B$4` for Lina?

   Why: 70 ÷ 200 = 0.35. B9 moved with the row, and $B$4 stayed.
   :::

2. Change Food in B9 from 70 to **80**. Which cells change by themselves?

   {{< record "The cells that changed: …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **B12** (total expenses 160), **B14** (left 40) and **C9** (0.4). You
   changed one number, and every formula that uses it changed.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Food goes from 70 to 80. What is left in B14 now?

   - [x] 40 JD

     Why: The expenses grow by 10 to 160, so 200 − 160 = 40.

   - [ ] 50 JD

     Why: B14 changes by itself when an expense changes.

   - [ ] 60 JD

     Why: More food means less left, not more.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="../../week-06/sims/budget-builder.html" poster="../../week-06/sims/budget-builder.png" title="Budget Builder: Sami's month" >}}

3. In **Budget Builder**, do the last two tasks: the part of food in C9,
   then the % button.

   {{< record "C9 shows … , then … with %" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **0.36** (90 ÷ 250), then **36 %** with the Percentage format: more
   than a third of Sami's money goes to food.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Why is there a `$` in `=B9/$B$4`?

   - [x] The total income stays the same in every row.

     Why: $B$4 is absolute: it does not move when you copy the formula.

   - [ ] The money is in dollars.

     Why: The $ sign of a reference has nothing to do with money.

   - [ ] It makes the result a percentage.

     Why: The % look comes from the number format.
   :::

## Experiment 3 · Make it readable: number formats

**The idea:** a **number format** changes how a number looks, not the
number itself (Home › Number). The parts get **Percentage** (0.35 looks
like 35%); the money gets **Number** with 2 decimals (50 looks like 50.00).
Make the Total lines bold, and widen a column that shows ####. The formula
bar always shows the real value.

**Aim:** make the budget easy to read, without changing its values.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (Excel)**
:::

1. Select C7:C11 and click **%** (Home › Number). Select B2:B14 and give it
   2 decimals (**Number** format). Make the two Total lines **bold**. Click
   C7 and look at the formula bar.

   {{< record "C7 shows … ; the formula bar shows …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   C7 shows **15%** (30 ÷ 200), but the formula bar still shows
   **=B7/\$B\$4**, and the value is 0.15. A format changes the look, not the
   value.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Does a number format change the value that the formulas use?

   - [x] No: it changes only the look; the value stays 0.15.

     Why: The formula bar shows the real value, so the formulas still work.

   - [ ] Yes: 15% becomes the number 15.

     Why: 15% is 0.15: the format only shows it as a percentage.

   - [ ] Yes: the decimals are deleted.

     Why: Fewer decimals on the screen do not change the value.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="../../week-06/sims/format-lab.html" poster="../../week-06/sims/format-lab.png" title="Number Format Lab: the same number, another look" >}}

2. In **Number Format Lab**, give the same number each format. What does
   0.36 look like in the Percentage format?

   {{< record "0.36 as a percentage looks like …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **36%**. In Currency with 2 decimals, 55 looks like **55.00 JD**. The
   value in the formula bar stays the same.
   :::

   ::: {.sort}
   Which format shows each look? Sort them.

   Percentage
   :   36%

       Why: 0.36 in the Percentage format.

   Number with 2 decimals
   :   55.00

       Why: Two decimals for money.

   A column that is too narrow
   :   ####

       Why: Make the column wider to see the number.
   :::
